Learning Types

Learning is a process that improves and enhances the knowledge of an artificial intelligence system by making observations about its environment.

Different Classes of Learning

  • Unsupervised Learning
    Learning without access to the desired output, known as 'teacher signals'.
    Examples are clustering, dimensionality reduction and association rules.

  • Supervised Learning
    Learning while also having access to the desired output.
    Examples are classification and regression.

  • Reinforcement Learning
    Learning via reward and punishment systems.
    Commonly used to train neural networks.

Clustering

Clustering is the means of separating a set of unsorted data points into subsets where the data in each subset shares a common proximity or trait.
This will often make use of a defined distance measure.

A cluster is a collection of objects that are similar in some way and dissimilar from objects belonging to other clusters.

  • A good example of clustering for everyday objects is categorising vehicles into clusters based on similarity.

  • The similarity metric could be the speed of the vehicle, or the size, or another property that allows separation of the individual objects.

  • These individual objects are referred to as data points.

Uses of Clustering

  • Clustering has many uses within modern technology including in genetic analysis and the arrangement of data for social media.
  • It is useful when there is no prior knowledge about the associations between data presented

Social Networks

  • Clustering is used extensively to arrange data about the interests of end-users.
  • This has uses in marketing, or the organisation of resources within a business.
  • Clusters may have stronger ties or weaker ties

Genetics

  • Clusters are very useful when understanding gene interactions.
  • This allows us to identify important genes linked to diseases.

Cluster Visualisation

  • An x-value and a y-value can be given to plotted points, where closer values mean greater similarity between the data.
  • Circular arrangements of a high data point density allow for visualising where clusters are located

Choosing a Metric

  • Choice of metric is dependent on the requirements of the data being analysed, depending on what is important
  • For some data, distance between points may be important. For other data, the distance/position may not matter, but the scale of difference might.

Embeddings

Embeddings involve mapping data into new space to capture varying characteristics. This is similar to the embeddings seen in large language models.

Spatial mappings can help visualise similarities and differences between data in a familiar context e.g. 3D space.

Clustering Algorithms: K-Means Clustering

Algorithm for K-Means

  • K, the number of clusters is a parameter determined by the user.
  • Centroids are initially defined positionally by the user, and are used to measure the distance between clusters.
  • Data points in visually mapped space will be assigned to the nearest centroid.
  • Once this is done, the centroids are be shifted to the centre of the allocated data points.
  • Data points are reassigned to new centroids.
  • This process is repeated until the data points converge.

Benefits and Drawbacks for K-Means

  • K-Means can be computationally faster than hierarchical clustering, if K is small.
  • It may also produce closer clusters than hierarchical clustering.
  • K-Means is not as effective for non-globular (non-round) clusters.
  • The use of a fixed number of (K) clusters may make it difficult to predict an optimal K value.

Clustering Algorithms: Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical Clustering Steps

  • Hierarchical Clustering will output a series of clustering results.
  • Each object starts in its own cluster, with clusters being repeatedly merged together.
  • By the end, all data points are in the same cluster
  • This allows for the creation of dendrograms which show the process flow of a hierarchical clustering run.
  • Merging clusters is more complex than merging individual data points.

Recomputing Distances: Merged Clusters

When merging clusters, a number of linkage methods can be tested and utilised.

  • Single Linkage: Involves finding the two closest data points between two clusters and merging them
  • Complete Linkage: Involves finding the two furthest data points between two clusters and merging them
  • Average Linkage: Involves finding the middle data points between two clusters and merging them.

Pros and Cons of Hierarchical Clustering

  • Hierarchical clustering is better for visual display than K-Means and works well for non-circular clusters.
  • Clusters created through hierarchical methods will typically be smaller than K-Means, allowing for tighter analysis of results
  • However, relocation of objects after merging is not possible so incorrect groupings cannot be fixed.
  • Use of different distance metrics in hierarchical clustering, may lead to different results.

Other Clustering Methods

  • Categorising data points may be difficult if data points can be allocated to multiple clusters. Fuzzifying can help with this problem - known as Fuzzy C-Means clustering.

Fuzzy Clustering

  • Cluster Membership is on a scale from 0 to 1, instead of data point cluster membership being absolute
  • Combination of clusters via centroid distance is multiplied by membership weight.

DBSCAN Clustering

  • Density Based Clustering method where data points are linked based on the radius around the points.
  • This is a highly effective method for clustering pre-processed image data.

Evaluating Cluster Quality

Verifying cluster quality is difficult since there is no defined correct result; learning is unsupervised.

Measures of cohesion and separation can be analysed to evaluate the effectiveness of clustering methods.

  • Cohesion: How tightly clustered are data points within a cluster?
  • Separation: How close are data points within different clusters?

Effective clustering will maximise cohesion and minimise separation.

Weighted-Kappa Metric

  • The Weighted-Kappa Metric can also be applied to evaluate a cluster set.
  • It is a scale between -1 and 1 where 1 means data is strongly clustered and 0 means not clustered at all.
  • The Kappa value should be between 0.8 and 1 to signify effective clustering.

Association Rules

  • Association Rules are a different form of unsupervised learning that works with sets instead of individual data points.
  • This involves trying to find different rules to determine which items go together
  • Association Rules are used extensively in supermarket data where points are grouped by similarity between what people buy. An example is the frequency of 2 items bought together e.g. milk, eggs
  • Sets of items can used to calculate different statistics - support, confidence and lift.
